Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

self noun

one’s own person

also one’s own self, not oneself, one’s usual self, self-love, self-confidence, know thyself

classical

Cic. Fin. 1.67: nisi aequē amīcōs et nōsmet ipsōs dīligāmus (Lewis & Short)
Hor. Ep. 1.2.33: ut tē ipsum servēs

ipse, ipsa, ipsum

pronoun

self, one’s very self (with the reflexive: sē ipsum, tē ipsum)

English “self” is a pronoun in Latin: the reflexive strengthened with ipse: tē ipsum, yourself; nōsmet ipsōs, ourselves (see oneself, myself, himself).

Other words

  • suī (genitive) — of oneself; self- (self-love, self-confidence)

    the genitive of the reflexive, after a noun · also used · classical · Hor. C. 1.18.14: caecus amor suī (Lewis & Short); Liv. 25.37.12: tanta fīdūcia suī (Lewis & Short, s.v. fīdūcia); Sen. Ben. 2.26.1: nēmō nōn benignus est suī jūdex (Lewis & Short)

    English compounds in self- are made with suī: amor suī, self-love; fīdūcia suī, self-confidence (Livy; Traupman 157 gives fīdūcia alone); suī jūdex, judge in one’s own case. For self-control see control.

  • suī similis — (being) one’s usual self, true to form

    similis with the genitive of the reflexive · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 3.2.16: quam uterque est similis suī! (Lewis & Short); Plaut. Trin. 2.2.7 (Lewis & Short)

    “Like himself”: just as he always is.

  • apud sē esse — to be oneself, in one’s right mind; nōn sum apud mē, I am not myself

    phrase: apud with the reflexive · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 4.4.85: Num tibi vidētur esse apud sēsē? (Lewis & Short); Ter. Haut. 5.1.48: prae īrācundiā, Menedēme, nōn sum apud mē (Lewis & Short)

    (vōx cōmica: Ter., Afran.)

    Literally “to be at home with oneself”. Mostly negative or with vix: not oneself, beside oneself with anger, fear or joy (Lewis & Short, s.v. apud).

Examples

  • cum igitur ‘nōsce tē’ dīcit, hoc dīcit: ‘nōsce animum tuum’

    so when he says “know yourself”, he means “know your soul”Cic. Tusc. 1.52 (Lewis & Short)

  • caecus amor suī

    blind love of selfHor. C. 1.18.14 (Lewis & Short)

  • quam uterque est similis suī!

    how like himself each of them is!Ter. Ph. 3.2.16 (Lewis & Short)

  • Num tibi vidētur esse apud sēsē?

    Does he seem to you to be himself?Ter. Hec. 4.4.85 (Lewis & Short)

  • Vix sum apud mē: ita animus commōtust metū, spē, gaudiō.

    I am hardly myself, my mind is so shaken by fear, hope and joy.Ter. And. 5.4.34 (Lewis & Short)

See also oneself, myself, himself, yourself, control, own.
